methodology_notes:
Item 1 was the hardest to apply consistently. The checklist names three specific things (last Thursday, the refactor, the 3% figure) that must each be treated as unverified input. W is the only output that explicitly hedges all three with clear language ('your reports, not verified facts', 'reported ~3%'). X hedges two explicitly and treats the third (3%) via quotation marks used in a hypothesis-fit context ('Fits "3%" and "started last Thursday" well') — I judged that as sufficient because it visibly flags the figure as an externally-supplied datum being tested rather than assumed, but this is a softer signal than W's and a different judge could reasonably score it absent. Y and Z each hedge only two of the three (Thursday and the refactor) and use the 3% figure as settled fact throughout, including Y explicitly and deliberately scoping its own hedge to 'two' statements — I scored both absent on strict no-partial-credit grounds, but note this produces a fairly severe read for two otherwise very careful outputs.

Item 4 was the second hardest call. W and Y both use explicit trigger/root-cause vocabulary in a dedicated passage. X and Z instead structure their fix sections as 'quick mitigation vs. durable fix', which does the same causal-reasoning work in spirit (don't stop at the surface event, fix the type-level defect underneath) but never names a 'trigger' as distinct from the defect in diagnostic terms. I scored X and Z absent because the checklist item is specifically about separating trigger from root cause in the diagnosis, not about sequencing a fix, but I flag this as a place where a more generous reading of 'satisfies the item in its own way' could flip both to present.

For the notable-error findings, the RSC-serialization claim in Z ('nothing throws at the boundary') is presented with more certainty than the topic supports, and is directly contradicted by hedges in W and Y on the same point; I treated this as a genuine substantive error worth flagging rather than a stylistic difference, since it is a concrete, checkable technical claim.
